claims.claim: To give a language individual flavour it must have woven into it the threads of an individual mythology.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Carl Hostetter, 'Tolkien's Invented Languages'
claims.quote: the threads of an individual mythology

claims.claim: The incarnate mind, the tongue and the tale are coeval; sub-creation is a birthright because we make as we are made.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Verlyn Flieger, 'On Fairy Stories'
claims.quote: We make, because we are made

claims.claim: The Lord of the Rings shows far more deliberate stylistic variation than any other novel, with sixty poems and songs in many styles and several languages.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Tom Shippey, 'The Lord of the Rings, Book of the Century'

claims.claim: A reader's essay argues Elrond's age is implied by archaic word order and that each character's speech stays consistent throughout, conveying culture and rank.
claims.source: K.G., 'To Make a Soul: Tolkien and Variations of Speech' (tolkienmedievalandmodern blog)
claims.quote: Elrond's age and sagacity implied through archaic word order

claims.claim: Moorcock holds that high fantasy's prose is the prose of the nursery-room, a lullaby meant to soothe, and that this is the predominant tone of The Lord of the Rings — the direct counter to Tolkien's claim to have shed the children's manner.
claims.source: Michael Moorcock, 'Epic Pooh' (1978; revolutionsf copy via Wayback)

claims.claim: Bratman and Williams reject Moorcock's reading of the prose as out of context and uninformed.
claims.quote: one wonders what book Moorcock read

claims.claim: Kullmann states on p. 111 that 85 per cent of the non-direct-speech (narrative) sections follow the point-of-view conventions of the nineteenth-century novel, i.e. are told from a hobbit's limited point of view.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: 85 per cent, of the non-direct-speech sections of the narrative

claims.claim: Wikipedia's sentence that the narrative is told '85% of the time' from one of the four hobbits' viewpoints is footnoted to Kullmann & Siepmann 2021 pp. 90-122; the figure itself sits on p. 111 of the 'Points of View' chapter.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Holmes reports that Kullmann measures the dominance of the hobbit point of view as 85% of all non-direct speech representing hobbits, and that the hobbits are the foci of 'psychonarration' (p. 105).
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)

claims.claim: Kullmann finds about 50 per cent of the text is dialogue, exclamations, embedded stories and recited poems, whereas in a novel direct speech would usually take up about 20 to 30 per cent (p. 90; repeated at p. 159).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: usually take up ca. 20 to 30 per cent

claims.claim: Wikipedia summarises K&S: about half of the novel is dialogue, poetry and song or embedded stories, against roughly 25% dialogue in a typical modern novel.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Bolding's review reports Kullmann's finding that direct speech comprises 50 percent of the text (K&S p. 90), with narrative oversight from the hobbits' point of view while keeping the third person.
claims.source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: using direct speech to comprise 50 percent of the text

claims.claim: Turner notes Kullmann's point that the proportion of direct speech is higher than usual in nineteenth- or twentieth-century novels because it serves purposes beyond social conversation and evokes older pre-texts.
claims.source: Allan Turner, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Inklings Studies 12.1 (2022)

claims.claim: Omniscient narration is comparatively rare; the reader is most commonly given the point of view of a group of characters, usually hobbits, before it narrows to an individual (p. 90).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.claim: The 'Points of View' chapter abstract: the narrator mostly presents the point of view of hobbits as a group or of Frodo, Sam, Pippin or Merry, and only to a far lesser extent Aragorn, Gimli, Legolas and Éowyn.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'Points of View' (ch. 4) abstract, Springer
claims.quote: to a far lesser extent Aragorn, Gimli, Legolas and Éowyn

verdicts.trueWording: To give your language an individual flavour
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched from tolkienestate.com. Page quotes Tolkien: “To give your language an individual flavour, it must have woven into it the threads of an individual mythology. … The converse indeed is true, your language construction will breed a mythology”. The cited quote string appears word for word; claim drops only the possessive ‘your’.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: ‘sub-creation is a birthright’ — the page never says sub-creation is a right or birthright (the word does not occur); it says only that we make because we are made in a Maker’s image
verdicts.trueWording: The incarnate mind, the tongue, and the tale, are coeval
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched. Coeval limb verbatim: ‘The incarnate mind, the tongue, and the tale, are in our world coeval’. The supplied quote is NOT contiguous on the page — it reads ‘We make, he said, “because we are made”’. Grep for birthright/right/inalienable across the whole page: zero hits.

verdicts.trueWording: far more deliberate stylistic variation than any other novel provides
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched. Both limbs on the page: ‘…if with far more deliberate stylistic variation than any other novel provides’ and ‘contains some sixty poems and songs, in many styles and several languages’. Only precision loss: the page hedges ‘some sixty’, the claim states ‘sixty’.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: ‘conveying … rank’ — the essay speaks of culture, nationality and personality; rank/status/class/station appear nowhere on the page
verdicts.trueWording: Elrond’s age and sagacity are implied through his archaic word order
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched (blogspot, live, 200). Author is a student signed ‘-- K.G.’, posted 18 April 2014 on the course blog Tolkien: Medieval and Modern — matches the source label. Consistency limb verbatim: ‘each character’s own speech is consistent throughout the entirety of The Lord of the Rings’. The supplied quote is a near-quote, not word for word (page has ‘are implied through his’).

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: ‘the direct counter to Tolkien’s claim to have shed the children’s manner’ — Moorcock’s page never mentions any such Tolkien claim; that clause is the researcher’s framing, not the source
verdicts.trueWording: prose of the nursery-room. It is a lullaby
verdicts.note: Live revolutionsf.com returns a 1-byte body (recovery route 1 failed); the 2026 Wayback capture is also empty; recovered via Wayback raw capture 20130328111451id_ (route 2), 42.8 KB of text, page header ‘Epic Pooh © Michael Moorcock’. Verbatim on the page: ‘The sort of prose most often identified with “high” fantasy is the prose of the nursery-room. It is a lullaby; it is meant to soothe and console.’ and ‘It is the predominant tone of The Lord of the Rings and Watership Down’. Every Moorcock-attributed limb is verbatim; only the trailing gloss is unsourced.

verdicts.trueWording: one wonders what book Moorcock read
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched. Bratman verbatim: ‘one wonders what book Moorcock read, because it’s certainly not The Lord of the Rings.’ plus ‘the fragments Moorcock quotes are “entirely out of context”’ (= out of context). Williams: ‘Moorcock has simply sneered at Tolkien without knowing what he is talking about’ (= uninformed). ‘of the prose’ is supported obliquely — the article frames Moorcock’s grounds as ‘the poverty of their writing style’ — though the word ‘prose’ appears in the article only in a navbox.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: raw page not reached — Google Books returns ‘Restricted Page / You have reached your viewing limit’; verdict rests on a search-within-volume snippet. Two further limbs are absent from that snippet: ‘point-of-view conventions’ (the snippet reads only ‘the conventions of the nineteenth-century novel’; phrase search for ‘point-of-view conventions’ returns 0) and the gloss ‘i.e. are told from a hobbit’s limited point of view’
verdicts.trueWording: 85 per cent, of the non-direct-speech sections of the narrative
verdicts.note: Google Books SearchWithinVolume on id=9uAsEAAAQBAJ returns 1 hit, page_number 111: ‘… 85 per cent, of the non-direct-speech sections of the narrative) follow the conventions of the nineteenth-century novel, as found in Ann Radcliffe and the Gothic novelists, in the novels of Walter Scott, Charles Dickens, George Eliot, Thomas Hardy…’. So the figure, the page number and the nineteenth-century-novel limb are corroborated; the snippet is truncated before the sentence’s subject, so the POV gloss cannot be checked. The volume TOC on the same page confirms ‘Points of View’ begins at p. 89, so p. 111 is inside ch. 4.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: ‘the figure itself sits on p. 111 of the “Points of View” chapter’ — the Wikipedia page says only pp. 90–122 and never mentions p. 111 (independently corroborated off-page via the Google Books p. 111 snippet, see index 634)
verdicts.trueWording: 85% of the time – one of the four Hobbit protagonists
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched. Sentence verbatim: ‘…most often – 85% of the time – one of the four Hobbit protagonists, Frodo, Sam, Merry, and Pippin.’ Footnote limb CONFIRMED from the HTML: the ref marker on that sentence carries id ‘cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKullmannSiepmann202190–122_7-0’ and the reference list entry reads ‘Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, pp. 90–122’.

Landing page carries only an abstract; the PDF is 403 on live scholar.valpo.edu even with a browser UA, referer and cookie jar (routes 1 and 3 failed). Recovered via Wayback raw capture 20221016142859id_ of the viewcontent.cgi PDF (route 2) and extracted with pypdf. Holmes writes: ‘Chapter 4 (“Points of View,” Kullmann) … measuring the dominance of the hobbit point of view in the novel by making them the internal storytellers (85% of all “non-direct” speech, according to Kullmann, represents hobbits), and the foci of “psychonarration (p. 105).’ Every limb verbatim; the only deviations are PDF-extraction spacing artifacts (‘85% o f all’, ‘non -direct’).

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: raw page not reached — Google Books shows ‘Restricted Page / You have reached your viewing limit’; the verdict rests on search-within-volume snippets, not the page itself
verdicts.trueWording: usually take up ca. 20 to 30 per cent of the text
verdicts.note: Every limb is corroborated by snippets, all on the claimed pages. p. 90: ‘… 50 per cent of the text is taken up by dialogues and exclamations as well as by stories told or poems recited by the characters.’ p. 90: ‘… usually take up ca. 20 to 30 per cent of the text.’ — the supplied quote word for word. p. 159: ‘… 50 per cent of the text is taken up by direct speech’, confirming the ‘repeated at p. 159’ limb. Downgraded solely by the snippet rule.

verdicts.trueWording: dialogue typically makes up around a quarter of the text
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched; no quote field supplied, so graded on substance. Page: ‘About half of The Lord of the Rings consists of dialogue, poetry and song, or stories told by a character. Thomas Kullmann and Dirk Siepmann … contrast it to the modern novel, where dialogue typically makes up around a quarter of the text.’ Every limb supported; ‘roughly 25%’ is the claim’s rendering of ‘around a quarter’.

verdicts.trueWording: using direct speech to comprise 50 percent of the text
verdicts.note: Landing page is abstract-only and the live PDF is 403; recovered via Wayback raw capture 20230512052131id_ of dc.swosu.edu viewcontent.cgi (route 2), extracted with pypdf. Bolding, Mythlore 41.1 p. 281: ‘Next, Thomas Kullmann takes over … the trilogy follows the standard patterns, using direct speech to comprise 50 percent of the text (90). Narrative oversight comes from the point of view of the hobbits and their experiences while even maintaining the third-person voice.’ Quote verbatim; the (90) citation and every limb check out.

verdicts.trueWording: higher proportion than is usual in nineteenth- or twentieth-century novels
verdicts.note: euppublishing.com returns a Cloudflare JS challenge on the live URL (route 1 failed); recovered via Wayback raw capture 20220615121435id_ (route 2). Byline confirms Allan Turner, Journal of Inklings Studies vol. 12 iss. 1, pp. 139–142, 2022. Page: ‘The next three chapters are devoted to direct speech, of which, as Kullmann points out, there is a higher proportion than is usual in either nineteenth- or twentieth-century novels, since it serves more purposes than straightforward social conversation, and indeed it mostly evokes pre-texts from an older period.’ No quote field was supplied, hence SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM; every limb is supported almost word for word.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: raw page not reached — Google Books shows only a search snippet; and within it the quoted opening word ‘omniscient’ is unconfirmed: ‘narration is comparatively rare’ hits p. 90, but ‘omniscient narration is comparatively rare’ returns 0 and ‘omniscient narration’ hits only pp. 103, 121, 123
verdicts.trueWording: narration is comparatively rare, the reader is most commonly treated
verdicts.note: Snippet, p. 90: ‘… narration is comparatively rare, the reader is most commonly treated to the point of view of a group of characters—hobbits, usually—before the perspective is narrowed down to a single person. The beginning of Chap. 1 provides an apt example…’ The substance of both limbs and the p. 90 citation are corroborated; the adjective before ‘narration’ is cut by the snippet’s leading ellipsis. Caution: Google’s phrase index here is demonstrably unreliable (‘comparatively rare’ returned 0 with the default index but 4 hits with newbks=0), so the 0-result is weak evidence of absence rather than a contradiction.

verdicts.trueWording: to a far lesser extent, Aragorn, Gimli, Legolas and Éowyn
verdicts.note: link.springer.com serves a Cloudflare ‘Client Challenge’ to curl (route 1 failed) and Crossref/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar all return a null abstract (routeHint-style DOI routes failed). Recovered via Wayback raw capture 20251019112825id_ of the chapter page (route 2). Abstract: ‘This chapter examines those parts of The Lord of the Rings which are written as a third-person narrative. Most of the time the narrator presents the point of view of a group of characters, usually hobbits, or a single character: Frodo, Sam, Pippin or Merry, or, to a far lesser extent, Aragorn, Gimli, Legolas and Éowyn.’ Quote word for word (page adds one comma after ‘extent’); independently mirrored on colab.ws.
